---
title: Writing Shell Scripts
---

Every command so far has been typed at the prompt, one line at a time. This
section is about putting those lines in a file instead.

A file of commands is called a **shell script**. The shell reads it and runs
the commands one after another, exactly as if you had typed them yourself. That
alone earns its keep: something you worked out once is something you never have
to work out again.

But a script is more than a saved transcript. The same script can do different
work each time it runs, because information reaches it from outside. There are
three ways in:

- **Arguments** --- the words typed after its name, the way `five.txt` is typed
  after `cat`
- **Standard input** --- whatever is typed at it or piped into it
- **The environment** --- values the shell hands to every program it starts,
  such as `$HOME`

Those are the same three channels that `cat`, `date` and every other command on
your system use. That is the point to hold on to as you go: a shell script is
not a lesser kind of program. By the end of this section yours will live in a
directory of its own, run by name from anywhere, with nothing to mark it out
from the commands that came with the machine.

## You will learn

- How to put commands in a file and run it
- How to pass arguments to a script, and repeat work with a loop
- How to make a script choose between two courses of action
- How to read input, whether typed at the keyboard or piped in
- What the environment is, and what a script inherits from it
- How to install a script so it works like any other command

## Before you start

You should be comfortable with `$name` and `$(command)` from
[The Dollar Sign](../the-dollar-sign.qmd). Scripts are where they begin to earn
their keep, and they turn up on nearly every page from here on.
